analysis.one_liner: Establishes a federal right to abortion, requires all health plans to cover it, and funds access grants.
analysis.headline: The Abortion Justice Act never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote in the Republican-controlled House, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a federal right to abortion and miscarriage care into law and let people sue any level of government that interferes with it. It would require every public and private health plan — Medicaid, Medicare, TRICARE, employer plans, marketplace plans — to cover abortion, strip federal conscience protections that let health facilities decline to provide or refer for it, put medication abortion on college campuses, and create a $350-million-a-year grant program covering the procedure plus travel, lodging, and childcare. It would also bar immigration arrests within 2,000 feet of any health facility and extend Medicaid and marketplace eligibility to immigrants with federally authorized presence.
analysis.who_benefits: People who need abortion care, especially those in the roughly 29 percent of states where it is banned or severely restricted, and the low-income patients, Medicaid and TRICARE enrollees, immigrants, and college students for whom cost and distance are the biggest barriers. It would also direct money to clinics, training programs, and doulas in underserved communities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People seeking abortion, especially in ban states

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a fundamental right to abortion and miscarriage care that federal, state, and local governments may not deny or penalize, enforceable by individuals through civil lawsuits against governments.

Requires every health program or plan — Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare, TRICARE, VA, federal employee, marketplace, and employer-sponsored private plans — to cover abortion with reimbursement sufficient to cover the cost, and repeals the ACA's abortion-coverage compromise (section 1303).

Authorizes $350 million a year in grants for direct abortion care, telehealth, provider training, patient travel and childcare costs, clinic construction and security, doulas, escorts, and legal help, prioritizing medically underserved communities.

Strikes the federal law (Public Health Service Act section 245) that shields health care entities from being required to perform or refer for abortion, and conditions all federal funding on facilities providing or referring for medically appropriate reproductive care; requires colleges receiving federal funds to offer medication abortion through student health centers, contracted providers, or telehealth.

Bars immigration enforcement actions by DHS, ICE, CBP, or state and local officers within 2,000 feet of any health care facility, and tightens HIPAA rules to prohibit sharing reproductive health information with law enforcement, including immigration officials, without authorization.

Removes the five-year waiting period for lawfully residing immigrants to get Medicaid and CHIP, and counts people with federally authorized presence (including deferred action) as lawfully present for marketplace subsidies, cost-sharing reductions, Medicaid, and CHIP.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund $350 million a year in grants. Health insurers and employers would bear the cost of mandated abortion coverage across every plan they offer. Religiously affiliated hospitals, clinics, and pharmacies would lose the ability to decline to provide or refer for abortion, and states with bans would lose the ability to enforce them against this federal right.

drawbacks.text: The coverage mandate reaches virtually every insurance plan in the country, including employer-sponsored and marketplace plans, and repeals the ACA compromise that let plans exclude abortion; premium costs would rise somewhat, and employers and states that currently exclude coverage could not opt out.

It overrides the conscience objections of religiously affiliated hospitals, clinics, and pharmacies by striking the federal refusal statute, conditioning all federal funds on providing or referring for abortion, and stating the Act is not subject to the Religious Freedom Restoration Act — a direct conflict with institutions that treat millions of patients.
The grant program costs $350 million every fiscal year with no sunset, on top of the cost of extending Medicaid, CHIP, and marketplace subsidies to previously excluded immigrant populations.

The bill lets individuals sue federal, state, and local governments, purports to strip state sovereign immunity, and says it supersedes all conflicting federal law — aggressive assertions of federal power over state abortion policy that would face immediate constitutional challenge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in the states where abortion is banned or severely restricted — the bill's findings say 29 percent of U.S. women of reproductive age — the access, coverage, and travel-cost provisions would be genuinely material, and the coverage mandate directly attacks the main financial barrier, which is cost. The costs are real but ordinary for an expansive health bill: modest premium increases from the coverage mandate, $350 million a year in grants, and the end of conscience protections for faith-based providers, which is the provision most likely to draw a constitutional challenge along with the immunity-stripping and supremacy language. It is a maximalist bill that leaves little room for the compromises that typically make health legislation passable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight committees on the day it was introduced, got bounced between Health subcommittee referrals three times, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on June 22, 2023, with four original cosponsors (Reps. Williams of Georgia, Escobar, Bush, and Frost).

The same day, it was referred to eight committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Natural Resources, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Accountability, and Foreign Affairs.

Its only further movement was three separate referrals to an Energy and Commerce subcommittee on Health, in June 2023, September 2023, and December 2024 — the last action of any kind before the Congress ended.
All 38 cosponsors were Democrats, 38 of the 216 House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored.
The bill never received a committee hearing or markup, and the Republican House majority never brought it to the floor; it expired on January 3, 2025, when the 118th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The governments and industries the bill would have regulated are better off because it died: states with abortion bans keep their laws, insurers and employers keep their coverage exclusions, and faith-based health facilities keep their refusal rights. People in restricted states gained nothing from the bill's death; the pre-Dobbs status quo of state-by-state access remained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States with bans, insurers, faith-based health systems

industries.note: The bill would fund clinic construction, security, broadband, staffing, and training, and would pay providers directly for care, travel support, and patient navigation at roughly adequate reimbursement rates. Clinics have been closing since Dobbs — the bill's findings cite 91 closures — so new money targets the access problem directly.

Every plan they sell, including employer-sponsored and marketplace plans, would be required to cover abortion with reimbursement sufficient to cover the cost, and the ACA's compromise exclusion would be repealed. The mandate's cost to the industry is the coverage patients gain.

The federal statute letting health entities refuse to perform or refer for abortion would be repealed, all federal funding would be conditioned on providing or referring for abortion, and the bill states it is not subject to the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. Institutions whose religious commitments conflict with that requirement would have to change practice or forgo federal funds.

Eligible employer-sponsored plans are expressly covered, so employers could no longer exclude abortion coverage; the added cost would land partly on premiums. Employees who want the coverage gain what the employer pays for.

Arrest and enforcement actions would be barred within 2,000 feet of any health care facility, limiting operations near clinics, pharmacies, and hospitals in border and interior checkpoint zones. The bill frames this as removing a chilling effect on care access.
